result:
No, this shouldn't go out as-is. There are three separate problems, and the PCI claim is the one that needs to stop you before anything else.

**"Fully compliant with PCI security standards"** — this is the highest-risk line. PCI DSS compliance isn't a property a piece of software can have on its own; it's an assessment of an entire cardholder-data environment (systems, processes, people) performed by a Qualified Security Assessor (QSA) or via self-assessment questionnaire, and it's scoped to a specific merchant/environment, not a library. A library can be *designed to support* PCI DSS requirements, but it cannot itself be "compliant." If a downstream user relies on this claim, fails their own PCI audit, and traces the false assurance back to your README, that's a real liability and false-advertising exposure. Don't publish this claim unless you actually have a QSA attestation backing it — and if you did, legal would already know.

**"Passed all our internal tests"** — vague and unverifiable, and it implies a level of assurance ("safe for production payment systems") that internal testing alone can't support, especially for something security-sensitive. If a vulnerability surfaces later, this sentence becomes evidence you overstated confidence.

**"MIT license... safe for anyone to use"** — this actually contradicts the MIT license itself. The MIT license text explicitly disclaims all warranties, including fitness for a particular purpose, and disclaims liability. Marketing "open and safe" language right next to a license that says "PROVIDED AS IS, WITHOUT WARRANTY OF ANY KIND" is internally inconsistent and undercuts the disclaimer you're relying on for liability protection.

**Suggested direction** (for legal to actually approve, not for me to finalize):
> "PayCheck is released under the MIT license. It has undergone internal testing and code review, and is built to align with PCI DSS best practices for handling payment data. As with any open-source software, users are responsible for evaluating its suitability and conducting their own security and compliance review before deploying it in production."

Flag this back to whoever wrote the draft — the PCI line in particular reads like it was written without input from someone who understands what PCI compliance actually certifies. I'd loop legal in before publishing, not just for a sanity check but to sign off on final wording.
